Since deposit it has grown three times, by Proposition~\ref{ad:dual}, the shifted torsion duality, by Proposition~\ref{aa:flux}, whose complete-flux normal form resolves Conjecture~\ref{ad4} true and proves the interval-support clause of Conjecture~\ref{ad3}, and by Proposition~\ref{ad:cover}, the subcritical direction of Conjecture~\ref{ad2}.  One identity is recorded as an uncounted remark rather than a conjecture: the insertion-power formula of Remark~\ref{ad:kraines}, whose source construction~\cite{LME24} computes an infinite family of higher operations for the torus that could not be compared in full through the present channel, with the attribution recorded where it occurs.  Conjectures~\ref{ad1} and~\ref{ad2} are stated in a random model; Conjectures~\ref{ad13} to~\ref{ad19} assert laws, the price of aiming at effective theorems in geometric analysis; Conjecture~\ref{ad19} is the part's closest to prior work, since the small-eigenvalue asymptotics of the induced K\"ahler degeneration metrics are now a theorem of~\cite{Cao26} and only the Ricci-flat, integrally LMHS-indexed content is claimed; and Conjecture~\ref{ad10} is possibly accessible from the existing wall geometry of~\cite{JM19}.

Throughout, the flux notation of Part~X is retained: $E_n(R)=\Lambda^{*}R^n$, and for $H\in\Lambda^r\Z^n$ of odd degree $r$, $d_H=H\wedge-$, with $b_k(H;R)$ the cohomology dimensions and $g_{n,r}$ the degreewise profile on the Zariski-open locus of maximal wedge ranks, so that $g_{n,3}=g_n$.  For the complete flux $H^{(n)}_\Delta$, $t_{p,k}(n)$ counts the $p$-primary cyclic summands of the integral cohomology in degree $k$, and $T_p(n)=\sum_kt_{p,k}(n)$.  A dimension $n$ is \emph{$r$-essential} when $g_{n,r}$ is not $(1+t)$ times the profile one dimension lower, so that a form ignoring one coordinate cannot saturate.  On the mirror side, configurations $\mathbf d$ and merges are as in Part~X; $D(\mathbf d)=\prod_id_i$, $\Lambda(\mathbf d)=\prod_id_i^{d_i}$; for the five one-parameter projective complete-intersection Calabi--Yau threefolds $(5)$, $(4,2)$, $(3,3)$, $(3,2,2)$, $(2,2,2,2)$, the mirror map $q_{\mathbf d}(z)=z+O(z^2)$, the genus-zero Gopakumar--Vafa invariants $N_{\mathbf d}(\beta)$, and the A-model Yukawa coupling $K_{\mathbf d}(q)=D(\mathbf d)+\sum_{\beta\ge1}N_{\mathbf d}(\beta)\beta^3q^\beta/(1-q^\beta)$ are the classical mirror data~\cite{HKTY95}, and $q_c(\mathbf d)$ is the smallest positive singularity of $K_{\mathbf d}$, the conifold point in the flat coordinate.

\begin{proposition}[Merge monotonicity and Chern floors]\label{ad:merge}
(i) Under every merge $d_i,d_j\mapsto d_i+d_j-1$, the degree $D$ strictly decreases and the scale $\Lambda$ strictly increases; in particular the algebraic conifold point $z_c=\Lambda^{-1}$ strictly decreases.  (ii) For a complete-intersection Calabi--Yau threefold of multidegree $\mathbf d$ in $\mathbb{CP}^{k-1}$, $k=\sum_id_i$, one has $c_2(X)\cdot H=\tfrac12\bigl(\sum_id_i^2-k\bigr)D$, so the ratios $\operatorname{td}_2(X)\cdot H/H^3$ for the five threefold configurations $(5)$, $(4,2)$, $(3,3)$, $(3,2,2)$, $(2,2,2,2)$ are $5/6$, $7/12$, $1/2$, $5/12$, $1/3$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) $d_id_j-(d_i+d_j-1)=(d_i-1)(d_j-1)>0$ gives the degree drop.  For $\Lambda$, the function $g(x)=x\log x$ is strictly convex with $g(1)=0$, and the pair $(d_i+d_j-1,\,1)$ has the same sum as $(d_i,d_j)$ with a strictly larger maximum, so majorization gives $g(d_i+d_j-1)>g(d_i)+g(d_j)$, which is $\log\Lambda'>\log\Lambda$.  (ii) From $c(TX)=(1+h)^k\prod_i(1+d_ih)^{-1}$, the degree-one term vanishes by the Calabi--Yau condition $\sum_id_i=k$, and the degree-two term is $\tfrac12(\sum_id_i^2-k)h^2$; multiplying by $H=h$ and integrating against the class of $X$, of degree $D$, gives the displayed value, and $\operatorname{td}_2=c_2/12$ with $H^3=D$ gives the five ratios $50/60$, $56/96$, $54/108$, $60/144$, $64/192$.
\end{proof}

\section{Odd flux and torsion shapes}

\begin{conjecture}[Odd-degree discrete saturation]\label{ad1}
Fix an odd $r\ge3$ and a finite symmetric $V\subset\Z\setminus\{0\}$ with $\gcd(V)=1$, and let every coefficient of $H_n\in\Lambda^r\Z^n$ be independent and uniform on $V$.  Then $\Pr[(b_k(H_n;\mathbb Q))_k=g_{n,r}]=1-O(e^{-cn})$ for some $c=c(r,V)>0$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
This lifts Conjecture~\ref{aa1} from three-forms to every odd degree, the full family in which wedge multiplication is a differential, against the Zariski-generic theory of~\cite{LN19}; the gcd normalization absorbs the scalar-invariance of rational ranks noted in Part~X.  The mechanism is anti-concentration for the structured minors of wedge multiplication, uniformly in the degree.  A first decisive theorem would be a uniform positive lower bound at $r=5$.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all sixty deposited dense $r=5$ trials and twenty-four independent trials at $n=9,10$ hit a single profile.  A counterexample would be an odd degree and a law with failure probability bounded away from zero.

\begin{conjecture}[Odd coverage-scale threshold]\label{ad2}
Fix odd $r\ge3$, include each coordinate $r$-subset independently with probability $p_n$, and give included monomials independent coefficients from a fixed finite symmetric nonzero set.  Along $r$-essential dimensions, $p_nn^{r-1}/\log n\to\infty$ implies saturation probability tending to one.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The isolated-vertex scale of random $r$-uniform hypergraphs is conjectured to govern saturation in every odd degree, with the $r$-essential restriction excluding exactly the suspension dimensions where an unused coordinate is harmless, the parity phenomenon noted in Part~X now built into the hypothesis.  The zero direction is now proved in Proposition~\ref{ad:cover}, a promotion, the essentiality hypothesis being exactly what an unused coordinate violates; the surviving supercritical direction is an extrapolation in the random model.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, deposited $r=5$ sweeps at $n=9,10$ rise from no hits to full saturation across the window.  A counterexample would be an essential sequence saturating below the scale or failing above it.

\begin{proposition}[Odd coverage threshold, zero direction]\label{ad:cover}
Fix an odd $r\ge3$ and an $r$-essential dimension $n$.  If $p_nn^{r-1}/\log n\to0$ then the saturation probability of Conjecture~\ref{ad2} tends to zero.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A coordinate lying in no chosen $r$-subset makes the profile $(1+t)h$ with $h$ the profile of the form read in the remaining $n-1$ coordinates, and the argument of Proposition~\ref{aa:support}(i), with $g_{n,r}$ in place of $g_n$, forces $h=g_{n-1,r}$ and $g_{n,r}=(1+t)g_{n-1,r}$ whenever such a form saturates; that is exactly what $r$-essentiality excludes.  A fixed coordinate is unused with probability $(1-p_n)^{\binom{n-1}{r-1}}$, which is $n^{-o(1)}$ when $p_nn^{r-1}=o(\log n)$, and two coordinates lie in only $O(n^{r-2})$ common $r$-subsets, so the second-moment estimate of Proposition~\ref{aa:support}(ii) applies verbatim and unused coordinates exist with probability tending to one.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Shifted torsion duality]\label{ad:dual}
For every prime $p$ and all $n,k$, $t_{p,k}(n)=t_{p,n+3-k}(n)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Write $u_k=b_k(H_\Delta;\mathbb F_p)-b_k(H_\Delta;\mathbb Q)$.  Since $d_{H_\Delta}$ raises degree by three, the universal coefficient theorem, applied to each residue class modulo three as an ordinary complex, gives $u_k=t_{p,k}(n)+t_{p,k+3}(n)$.  The perfect pairing $\Lambda^k\times\Lambda^{n-k}\to\Lambda^n\cong\Z$ intertwines $d_{H_\Delta}$ with its own transpose up to sign, since $H_\Delta\wedge\alpha\wedge\beta=\pm\,\alpha\wedge H_\Delta\wedge\beta$, so over every field $b_k=b_{n-k}$ and hence $u_k=u_{n-k}$.  Setting $s_k=t_{p,n+3-k}(n)$, the identity in degree $n-k$ reads $s_k+s_{k+3}=u_k=t_{p,k}(n)+t_{p,k+3}(n)$; both sequences vanish for $k\le2$, since no differential enters below degree three, and beyond degree $n$, so induction in steps of three gives $t_{p,k}(n)=s_k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{conjecture}[Torsion shape law for the complete flux]\label{ad3}
For every prime $p$ and every $n$, every interior positive triple of $k\mapsto t_{p,k}(n)$ is strictly log-concave.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Part~X's staircase, Conjecture~\ref{aa7}, locates the onset of $p$-torsion; this asserts the complete degreewise shape of the torsion once present, an integral refinement invisible to every field coefficient, in the twisted-cohomology setting whose integral theory is developed in~\cite{LME24}.  The duality centre $\tfrac{n+3}2$ sits half a step above Poincar\'e symmetry, the shift produced by the degree-three differential.  The duality clause is proved in Proposition~\ref{ad:dual} and the interval-support clause in Proposition~\ref{aa:flux}, which identifies the support as the full range $2p+1\le k\le n-2p+2$; both are now proved, and strict log-concavity is the surviving clause.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, every nonzero profile through $n=12$ at $p=2,3,5$ passed all three clauses in an independent exact-rank recomputation, including the profiles $1,10,44,10,1$ at $n=11$ and $1,11,54,54,11,1$ at $n=12$, and a recomputation from the normal form extends the log-concavity check to every prime $p\le23$ through $n=150$ without a failure.  A counterexample would be a flat interior triple at any prime.

\begin{conjecture}[Post-onset torsion persistence, resolved true]\label{ad4}
For every prime $p$, $T_p(n+1)>T_p(n)$ for every $n\ge4p-1$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The staircase of Conjecture~\ref{aa7} never retreats: once $p$-torsion appears it grows strictly with the dimension, so each prime contributes a permanently expanding sector of torsion flux charge.  Conditional on the totals of Conjecture~\ref{aa6}, the $p=2$ case was already a theorem, now sharpened: the increments reduce to $4^{m-1}-\frac m{m+1}\binom{2m}m$ and its even companion, both positive from $m=3$ with the small cases checked directly.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, the independent recomputation gives $T_2=1,2,10,20,66,132$ from $n=7$ to $12$ and $T_3=1,2$ at $n=11,12$, and the closed-form $p=2$ expression increases strictly through $n=200$.  A counterexample would be one prime and one dimension with stagnant total torsion.  \emph{Resolution.} The conjecture is true for every prime, not only conditionally at $p=2$: Proposition~\ref{aa:flux} gives $T_p(2g+2)=2T_p(2g+1)$ from the null vector in even dimension and $T_{g+1}-2T_g=\sum_{r\ge1}\binom g{r-1}2^{g+1-r}A_r>0$ from Pascal's rule in odd dimension, both strict after onset.  An independent recomputation confirms strict growth for every prime $p\le11$ through dimension $150$.

\begin{remarkx}[Insertion powers of the complete flux]\label{ad:kraines}
The integral twisting theory of~\cite{LME24} attaches to a three-form its insertion powers, odd-degree forms driving an extended differential in the manner of Kraines' higher Massey powers~\cite{Kra66}.  Exact enumeration of the signed regular families on $2m+1$ labels gives, for $m\le4$, the identity that the $m$-th insertion power of the complete three-form is $(-1)^{m-1}(2m+1)^{m-1}$ times the complete $(2m+1)$-form, a Cayley-like coefficient collapsing a sum of $76{,}545$ terms at $m=4$.  Since~\cite{LME24} computes an infinite family of higher operations for the torus that could not be compared in full through the present channel, the identity is recorded here as a verified calibration observation with its attribution unresolved, and is not counted among the conjectures.
\end{remarkx}

\section{Quantum monotonicity along the merge order}

\begin{conjecture}[Normalized mirror-map contraction]\label{ad5}
For complete-intersection Calabi--Yau $n$-folds with $n\ge3$, write $\hat q_{\mathbf d}(x)=\Lambda(\mathbf d)\,q_{\mathbf d}(x/\Lambda(\mathbf d))=x+\sum_{m\ge2}c_m(\mathbf d)x^m$.  Under every merge, $c_m(\mathbf d')\le c_m(\mathbf d)$ for every $m\ge2$, with strict inequality for every $m\ge3$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The mirror map is the transcendental heart of the classical mirror computations~\cite{HKTY95,Zin14}, and the conjecture asserts that in the scale-free normalization fixed by $\Lambda$, whose merge growth is the proved half of Proposition~\ref{ad:merge}, equation consolidation contracts every coefficient at once; the two-fold violations found in the deposited scan are excluded by the dimension hypothesis, and the $m=2$ equalities at $n=3$ fix the non-strict boundary exactly.  A first decisive theorem would be the $m=2$ case in every dimension.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, the deposited scan through dimension nine and order eight passed off dimension two, and an independent exact recomputation of all merges in dimensions three to five, $588$ comparisons, found zero violations.  A counterexample would be one merge and one order breaking the contraction.

\begin{conjecture}[Gopakumar--Vafa amplification]\label{ad6}
For the five one-parameter threefold configurations and every merge edge, $A_\beta=N_{\mathbf d'}(\beta)/N_{\mathbf d}(\beta)$ is strictly increasing in $\beta\ge1$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Coefficientwise growth of curve counts under merges would already be a shape law; monotonicity of the ratio is much sharper, an ordering of the five geometries by quantum growth rate that refines degree-by-degree.  The mechanism is the conifold hierarchy of Conjecture~\ref{ad8} propagated backward through Conjecture~\ref{ad7}.  A first decisive theorem would be the asymptotic ratio divergence from separated conifold radii.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, deposited exact invariants through $\beta=60$ and an independent from-scratch mirror computation through $\beta=24$ agree and pass on all five edges, the amplification rising from $1.41$ at $\beta=1$ to $10^{15}$ scale at high degree on the steepest edge.  A counterexample would be one edge and one degree with a falling ratio.

\begin{conjecture}[Monotone conifold approach]\label{ad7}
For each of the five configurations, $R_\beta=N(\beta+1)/N(\beta)$ is strictly increasing, and $R_\beta\to1/q_c$; equivalently the invariants are strictly log-convex from degree one with ratio limit the conifold growth constant.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
That the conifold point governs the exponential growth rate of genus-zero invariants is folklore of the resurgence and enumerative literature; the content here is global monotonicity from the first degree, an unexpectedly rigid convexity of the full quantum series with no preasymptotic dip anywhere in the landscape's simplest column.  A first decisive theorem would be log-convexity in large degree from the conifold expansion.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, deposited invariants through $\beta=60$ and the independent recomputation through $\beta=24$ are strictly log-convex for all five families, with final tested ratios still below the independently computed constants $1/q_c=1980.15$, $641.78$, $458.89$, $269.61$, $159.26$.  A counterexample would be one family and one degree with a falling ratio.

\begin{conjecture}[Merge monotonicity of the conifold constant]\label{ad8}
For every merge edge among the five configurations, $q_c(\mathbf d')<q_c(\mathbf d)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The algebraic conifold point $z_c=\Lambda^{-1}$ decreases under merges by Proposition~\ref{ad:merge}; the conjecture asserts that the transcendental image under the mirror map preserves this order, so that consolidation strictly raises the quantum growth constant $1/q_c$.  This is a comparison of periods across distinct Picard--Fuchs systems, not a formal consequence of the algebraic ordering.  A first decisive theorem would be one edge by interval arithmetic on the hypergeometric sums; indeed the whole five-edge statement is a finite certification target for validated numerics, and should eventually be a computation rather than a conjecture.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, independent sixty-digit evaluations of the five constants order strictly along every edge, with ratios of consecutive constants between $1.69$ and $4.32$.  A counterexample would be one edge with reversed constants.

\begin{conjecture}[Conifold-normalized Yukawa monotonicity]\label{ad9}
For every merge edge among the five configurations and every $0<x<1$, $K_{\mathbf d'}(xq_c(\mathbf d'))/D(\mathbf d')>K_{\mathbf d}(xq_c(\mathbf d))/D(\mathbf d)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
At the same fraction of the respective conifold radii, the quantum-corrected Yukawa coupling normalized by its classical intersection number strictly increases under consolidation: a scale-free comparison of quantum corrections across geometries in which both normalizations are essential, since the deposited adversarial control shows the raw instanton comparison reversing at every grid point.  A first decisive theorem would be the small-$x$ regime from degree-one invariants alone.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $495$ deposited grid tests and an independent recomputation on all five edges at nineteen fractions passed, with the raw-instanton control failing everywhere, retained in place.  A counterexample would be one edge and one fraction with a reversed normalized coupling.

\section{Stability walls and sharp constants}

\begin{conjecture}[Quadratic wall complexity]\label{ad10}
Let $X$ be a Picard-rank-one Calabi--Yau threefold with a constructed component $\operatorname{Stab}^\dagger(X)$ satisfying the support property, $K$ a compact set in a fundamental domain for the $\widetilde{\mathrm{GL}}_2^+(\mathbb R)$ action, and $\|\cdot\|$ a Euclidean norm on the numerical charge lattice.  Then there is $C_K$ with $N_K(v)\le C_K(1+\|v\|)^2$ for every primitive charge $v$, where $N_K(v)$ counts numerical walls for $v$ meeting $K$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Local finiteness of walls is classical~\cite{BM22}, and the Picard-rank-one wall geometry of~\cite{JM19} bounds the largest walls and proves finiteness in bounded regions.  On a compact set the support property bounds each possible destabilising class by $O_K(\|v\|)$, which gives a polynomial count.  In the usual rank-four numerical charge lattice, a naive count after quotienting by the direction of $v$ is cubic rather than quadratic.  The exponent two therefore needs genuine Picard-rank-one wall geometry and does not follow merely because a wall is a quadric.  A first decisive theorem would isolate the extra geometric restriction that removes one lattice degree of freedom.  A counterexample would be a charge sequence with superquadratic wall counts in a fixed compact region.

\begin{conjecture}[Sharp $\Gamma$ for Brill--Noether stability]\label{ad11}
For a Picard-rank-one complete-intersection Calabi--Yau threefold covered by the Brill--Noether construction of~\cite{FKLR25}, with $\varepsilon_*$ the supremum of $\varepsilon$ for which their condition $\mathrm{BG3}(\varepsilon)$ holds, the infimum of $\gamma$ for which $\Gamma=\gamma H^2-\operatorname{td}_2(X)$ satisfies the $\Gamma$-twisted Bayer--Macr\`i--Toda ($\Gamma$-BMT) stability condition is exactly $\max\{4/(H^3\varepsilon_*),\ \operatorname{td}_2(X)\cdot H/H^3\}$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The construction of~\cite{FKLR25} proves that $\mathrm{BG3}(\varepsilon)$ yields a valid $\Gamma$ on this ray and leaves its minimization open; the conjecture asserts their bound is already the exact optimum, so the Brill--Noether route loses nothing.  The sharpness direction is the exposed half: it requires destabilizing objects at every smaller $\gamma$, a converse the construction itself does not supply.  The topological floor $\operatorname{td}_2\cdot H/H^3$ is unconditional, and Proposition~\ref{ad:merge} computes it as $5/6$, $7/12$, $1/2$, $5/12$, $1/3$ across the five configurations.  A first decisive theorem would be optimality of the floor branch for the quintic.  A counterexample would be a valid $\Gamma$ strictly below the displayed maximum.

\begin{conjecture}[Tame wall atlas]\label{ad12}
For $X$ as in Conjecture~\ref{ad10} and compact $K$, fix a finite effective $\mathbb R_{\mathrm{an},\exp}$ presentation of the central charge and the numerical wall equations.  Let formula format record length, quantifier depth, polynomial degree and logarithmic coefficient height in that presentation.  There is $C=C(X,K)$ such that the union $W_Q$ of numerical walls for primitive charges with $\|v\|\le Q$ has a defining formula of format at most $Q^C$, and $K\setminus W_Q$ has a compatible definable stratification into $O(Q^C)$ strata and chambers.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
This imports the definability paradigm of arithmetic Hodge theory~\cite{BKT20} into Bridgeland geometry.  Qualitative o-minimal definability alone supplies neither a canonical format nor a polynomial chamber bound.  The statement therefore fixes the presentation and treats polynomial formula format and polynomial stratification count as separate claims.  The numerical-wall formulation is essential because actual walls can accumulate.  A first decisive theorem would give an effective definition and a quantitative cell decomposition for one wall family.  A counterexample would be a wild wall arrangement or superpolynomial stratum growth.

\section{Effective geometry of Calabi--Yau families}

\paragraph{Gauge convention.}
Two positive gauges $\delta$ and $\delta'$ on the smooth locus of a fixed compact semialgebraic chart are \emph{power-equivalent} if, after truncation to $(0,1]$, there are positive constants $c,C,a,b$ with $c\delta^a\le\delta'\le C\delta^b$.  Every polynomial estimate below is understood up to this equivalence.  The gauge $\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is represented by a truncated norm of generators of the reduced discriminant ideal.  For a family of bundle pairs, $\delta_{\mathrm{pair}}$ is represented by the minimum of $\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}$ and a fixed positive stability margin that vanishes exactly on the chosen chamber boundary.

\begin{conjecture}[Polynomial conditioning of Ricci-flat metrics]\label{ad13}
For a projective polarised Calabi--Yau family over a compact semialgebraic chart, with $\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}$ the truncated norm of generators of the reduced discriminant ideal, the volume-normalised Ricci-flat metrics satisfy, for every derivative order $\ell$, bounds $\|\nabla^\ell\mathrm{Rm}\|_\infty\le C_\ell\,\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}^{-A_\ell}$, with diameter bounded by $C\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}^{-A}$ and, in the noncollapsing case, injectivity radius bounded below by $C^{-1}\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}^{A}$, the same polynomial form holding for the regularity scale in collapsing strata away from the canonical collapsing set.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Diameter bounds at degeneration are now sharp in the degeneration parameter~\cite{Li20}, and quantitative collapse is understood in important families~\cite{SZ19}; the conjecture asserts the global effective statement, polynomial control of all curvature derivatives in an algebraic gauge, the form of estimate that certifies every numerical metric computation at once.  \L ojasiewicz inequalities make the gauge canonical up to the exponents.  A first decisive theorem would be the curvature bound for one-parameter quintic degenerations.  A counterexample would be a family with essential superpolynomial blow-up in the algebraic gauge.

\begin{conjecture}[Discriminant-effective balanced convergence]\label{ad14}
In the setting of Conjecture~\ref{ad13}, the level-$k$ balanced metrics satisfy $\|g_{s,k}-g_s\|_{C^\ell(g_s)}\le C_\ell\,\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}(s)^{-A_\ell}k^{-1}$ whenever $k\ge C_\ell\,\delta_{\mathrm{alg}}(s)^{-B_\ell}$, with the corresponding $k^{-N-1}$ bounds after subtracting $N$ Bergman expansion terms.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
On a fixed smooth fiber this is classical Bergman asymptotics; the conjecture makes the rate uniform in the family with polynomial deterioration at the discriminant, exactly the regime probed by the balanced-metric power laws observed numerically near large complex structure~\cite{BHJMM26}.  A first decisive theorem would be the $C^0$ case near a conifold degeneration.  A counterexample would be a family where the required level grows faster than any power of the inverse algebraic distance.

\begin{conjecture}[Discriminant-effective Hermitian--Yang--Mills convergence]\label{ad15}
For an algebraic family of polarised Calabi--Yau threefolds with slope-stable bundles on a constant-stability chamber, with $\delta_{\mathrm{pair}}$ as in the gauge convention, the level-$k$ balanced-bundle approximations converge to the Hermitian--Yang--Mills connection in Coulomb gauge with $\|A_{s,k}-A_s\|_{C^\ell}\le C_\ell\,\delta_{\mathrm{pair}}^{-A_\ell}k^{-1}$ whenever $k\ge C_\ell\,\delta_{\mathrm{pair}}^{-B_\ell}$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Hermitian--Yang--Mills existence survives conifold transitions~\cite{Chu12}, iteration on a fixed stable bundle converges~\cite{CSYZ26}, and the numerical algorithms are mature~\cite{ABKO10}; the conjecture is the missing family statement, a polynomial condition number in distance to where the fiber or the stability degenerates.  A first decisive theorem would be the fixed-fiber statement with explicit stability-margin dependence.  A counterexample would be a chamber whose HYM approximation cost is essentially superpolynomial at the boundary.

\begin{conjecture}[Polynomial matter spectral gap]\label{ad16}
In the setting of Conjecture~\ref{ad15}, for a representation and form degree with locally constant bundle cohomology, the smallest positive eigenvalue of the bundle-valued Dolbeault Laplacian satisfies $\lambda_+(s)\ge C^{-1}\delta_{\mathrm{pair}}(s)^{A}$, simultaneously for any fixed finite list of representations and degrees.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Bundle-valued spectra are computable numerically~\cite{Ash24,AHHO23} and rigorous eigenvalue floors are an explicitly wanted certificate in that programme; the conjecture asserts the floor is polynomial in the algebraic gauge, with the constant-cohomology hypothesis essential since a jump lets an eigenvalue cross zero.  A first decisive theorem would be the scalar case on quintics near a conifold.  A counterexample would be an admissible chamber with essentially exponential spectral collapse.

\begin{conjecture}[Certified heterotic Yukawa convergence]\label{ad17}
Under Conjectures~\ref{ad13} to~\ref{ad16}, the level-$k$ physical heterotic Yukawa couplings satisfy $|Y^{(k)}_{abc}/Y_{abc}-1|\le C\,\delta_{\mathrm{pair}}^{-A}\delta_Y^{-A}k^{-1}$ for $k\ge C\delta_{\mathrm{pair}}^{-B}\delta_Y^{-B}$, where $\delta_Y$ is the power-equivalence class of a truncated algebraic gauge for the zero locus of the corresponding holomorphic coupling.  An absolute error bound of the same form holds with no $\delta_Y$ factor.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Physical Yukawa couplings and even quark masses are now computed numerically from learned geometric data~\cite{But24,Con24}, with only a-posteriori error diagnostics; the conjecture asserts the a-priori certificate, relative error polynomial in the two algebraic gauges, the $\delta_Y$ factor being necessary because no uniform relative bound can survive a coupling crossing zero.  A first decisive theorem would be the absolute bound for a single standard-embedding coupling.  A counterexample would be an admissible family whose certified level grows faster than any power.

\section{Degenerations and towers}

\begin{conjecture}[Saturation-index special-Lagrangian realization]\label{ad18}
For a semistable one-parameter Calabi--Yau threefold degeneration of type II, III, or IV with unipotent monodromy, let $L_{\mathrm{orb}}$ be the nilpotent-orbit lattice of asymptotically light D3 charges of common limiting phase, $L_{\mathrm{sat}}$ its rational saturation in integral homology, and $I_\tau$ the exponent of $L_{\mathrm{sat}}/L_{\mathrm{orb}}$.  Every primitive charge generating an extremal ray of the saturated light cone with the required positive limiting phase has a multiple $m\gamma$, with $m$ dividing $I_\tau$, admitting a calibrated special-Lagrangian representative for all sufficiently deep parameters.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Special-Lagrangian towers are constructed in Tyurin limits~\cite{HMWW26} and the type II--III--IV asymptotics are developed in~\cite{MWW26}; the new clause is arithmetic, the divisor bound $m\mid I_\tau$ tying calibrated existence to the saturation exponent of the monodromy-orbit lattice, so that the failure of primitive realization is quantized by lattice theory.  At $I_\tau=1$ the statement reduces to primitive realization.  Extremality of the ray is the stability surrogate: a light charge on an extremal ray admits no decomposition into non-proportional light charges of the common phase, and decay channels involving heavy charges are excluded deep in the limit by mass comparison, so the wall-crossing obstructions that block naive realization claims are switched off by hypothesis.  A first decisive theorem would be the type II case with $I_\tau=1$.  A counterexample would be an extremal ray whose minimal calibrated multiple fails to divide the saturation exponent.

\begin{conjecture}[LMHS-controlled Laplace towers]\label{ad19}
For a semistable one-parameter polarised Calabi--Yau degeneration at infinite Weil--Petersson distance, fix a normalisation of $d_{\mathrm{WP}}$ and volume-normalise the Ricci-flat metrics.  The vanishing scalar Laplace spectrum admits a finite partition into tower types $a$ with rational exponents $\alpha_a$ such that:
(i) the list of exponents depends only on the isomorphism class of the integral limiting mixed Hodge structure and the combinatorial dual-intersection and essential-skeleton data.
(ii) for each tower there is a positive normalizer $N_a(t)=e^{2\alpha_ad_{\mathrm{WP}}(t)}\ell_a(t)$, with $\ell_a$ slowly varying in $e^{d_{\mathrm{WP}}(t)}$, such that for every fixed $j$ the quantity $N_a(t)\lambda_{a,j}(t)$ converges to the $j$-th eigenvalue of a canonical weighted Laplace operator on the collapsed base geometry.
(iii) with eigenvalues labelled in increasing order at each parameter, every fixed-rank eigenvalue branch tending to zero belongs eventually to one of these towers.
The limiting operator may depend on the canonical metric data of the collapsed base and is not asserted to be determined by the limiting mixed Hodge structure alone.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
For induced K\"ahler degeneration metrics, exact small-eigenvalue rates are now a theorem of~\cite{Cao26}.  General skeleton-Laplacian convergence is not.  The conjecture makes three stronger claims for volume-normalised Ricci-flat metrics.  It asserts a finite exhaustive tower decomposition, an arithmetic classification of the rational exponents by the integral limiting mixed Hodge structure and skeleton combinatorics, and spectral convergence within each tower.  Only the exponent list is claimed to be determined by that discrete data.  The slowly varying normalizer is deliberate: metric collapse is known to generate logarithmic scales, and only regular variation in the Weil--Petersson gauge is asserted.  The limiting operator is allowed to retain canonical metric information from the collapsed base.  A first decisive theorem would establish the finite decomposition for a type IV maximal degeneration.  A counterexample would be a light eigenvalue escaping every listed tower or an exponent varying while the stated discrete data remain fixed, or a tower whose normalizer fails regular variation.

\part{Convexity, defect, and dispersion laws for projective invariants}

\medskip\noindent\emph{Added to the deposit: 19 August 2026.}\par\medskip

The fifteen conjectures below take three of the oldest invariants of projective algebraic geometry, the middle cohomology of a complete intersection, the graded Betti table of an embedded surface, and the Hodge decomposition of a hypersurface, and conjecture the discrete shape of each as its defining degrees move.  They form three programmes.  A convexity programme (Conjectures~\ref{ae1} to~\ref{ae6}) studies the degree-normalized primitive middle Betti number of smooth complete intersections on the full multidegree lattice, asserting a coherent discrete-convexity package: coordinate monotonicity and convexity, supermodular absolute interaction with log-submodular relative interaction, Schur-convexity at fixed degree sum, and a strict decrease under every codimension-raising split that preserves the adjunction coefficient.  A syzygy programme (Conjectures~\ref{ae7} to~\ref{ae11}) studies the two nontrivial rows of the Betti tables of $\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1$ under Segre--Veronese embeddings, replacing global shape claims by a controlled-defect law: the nonlinear row is strictly log-concave, while the linear row can fail log-concavity at most once, only past its mode, only where the nonlinear row is already present, and only within one step of that row's mode.  A dispersion programme (Conjectures~\ref{ae12} to~\ref{ae15}) studies the normalized primitive Hodge profiles of smooth hypersurfaces as the degree grows, asserting that the known drift toward the Eulerian profile is monotone in four canonical stochastic orders: likelihood-ratio flattening, central-window escape, convex-order spread, and total-variation distance.  The proved layer is five propositions: Proposition~\ref{ae:curve} proves all six convexity laws for curves from the exact formula $B=\sum_id_i-c-2+2/D$, Proposition~\ref{ae:strand} pins the two syzygy rows to the Hilbert series by an exact antidiagonal identity, Proposition~\ref{ae:surface} proves all four dispersion laws for surfaces from an explicit rational function of the degree, Proposition~\ref{ae:hyper} proves the coordinate monotonicity and convexity laws of Conjectures~\ref{ae1} and~\ref{ae2} for hypersurfaces in every dimension from a closed form, and Proposition~\ref{ae:disp} derives Conjectures~\ref{ae13} and~\ref{ae14} from the likelihood-ratio flattening of Conjecture~\ref{ae12}; in addition, for odd $n$ the Calabi--Yau slice of Conjecture~\ref{ae6} is already a corollary of the merge monotonicity of Proposition~\ref{x:merge}.  Two negative controls are retained in place: the unnormalized primitive Betti number fails Schur-convexity and has no split direction already for curves and surfaces, and coordinatewise monotone convergence to the Eulerian limit fails at dimension twelve, so the normalization of the convexity programme and the total-variation formulation of the dispersion programme are both forced.  Conjectures~\ref{ae7} to~\ref{ae11} rest on the thirteen complete published tables, the entire deposited corpus, and are resting on a small evidence base; Conjecture~\ref{ae7} sits closest to the published unimodality conjecture of~\cite{BCEGLY22} and is the part's closest to prior work; Conjectures~\ref{ae12} to~\ref{ae15} assert laws at every degree and dimension, and the Eulerian limit itself is exact in the abelian setting of~\cite{LS25} and asymptotic in the toric setting of~\cite{DK86}, so only the monotone interpolation is claimed as new.

For a smooth complex complete intersection $X^n(\mathbf d)\subset\mathbf P^{n+c}$ of dimension $n\ge1$, codimension $c\ge1$, and multidegree $\mathbf d=(d_1,\ldots,d_c)$ with every $d_i\ge2$, write $D(\mathbf d)=\prod_id_i$; the Lefschetz theorem confines the new topology to the middle degree, and the primitive middle Betti number is $b_n^{\mathrm{prim}}=(-1)^n(\chi(X)-(n+1))$ with $\chi$ evaluated exactly by the Chern-class formula $\chi=D\,[H^n](1+H)^{n+c+1}/\prod_i(1+d_iH)$~\cite{GL02,CO74}.  The invariant of the convexity programme is the \emph{degree-normalized primitive complexity} $B_{n,c}(\mathbf d)=b_n^{\mathrm{prim}}/D(\mathbf d)$, and $e_i$ denotes a coordinate step in the multidegree lattice.  For the Segre--Veronese embedding of $\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1$ by $\mathcal O(a,b)$ with $a,b\ge2$, in characteristic zero, the graded Betti numbers $\beta_{p,p+q}(a,b)$ of the homogeneous coordinate ring vanish outside $q=0,1,2$; write $\Delta^{(q)}_p=\beta_{p,p+q}^2-\beta_{p-1,p-1+q}\beta_{p+1,p+1+q}$ for the log-concavity determinant at an interior index of the $q$th row, call $p$ a \emph{defect} of the row when $\Delta^{(q)}_p<0$, and let $m_q$ be the least index at which the row attains its maximum.  For a smooth hypersurface $X^n_d\subset\mathbf P^{n+1}$ with $n\ge2$, $d\ge3$, the primitive Hodge numbers are $h_p(n,d)=[t^{(p+1)d-(n+2)}](1+t+\cdots+t^{d-2})^{n+2}$ by Griffiths' formula~\cite{Gri69}; write $\pi_{n,d}$ for the normalized profile $h_p/\sum_jh_j$ on $\{0,\ldots,n\}$, symmetric about $n/2$, and $\varepsilon_n(p)=A(n+1,p)/(n+1)!$ for the Eulerian profile, with $A$ the Eulerian numbers.  A profile $P$ precedes $Q$ in \emph{convex order} when $\mathbf E\varphi(P)\le\mathbf E\varphi(Q)$ for every convex $\varphi$, and $\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\tfrac12\sum_p|P(p)-Q(p)|$.

\begin{proposition}[Curve calibration for the convexity programme]\label{ae:curve}
For $n=1$ one has $B_{1,c}(\mathbf d)=\sum_id_i-c-2+2/D$, and all six laws of Conjectures~\ref{ae1} to~\ref{ae6} hold strictly for curves.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The genus formula for complete-intersection curves gives $b_1=D(\sum_id_i-c-2)+2$, whence the displayed $B$.  Write $u=2/D$.  For Conjecture~\ref{ae1}, a step in $d_i$ adds $1$ to the linear part and changes $u$ by $-2/(D(d_i+1))$, so $\Delta_iB=1-2/(D(d_i+1))\ge1-\tfrac13>0$.  For Conjecture~\ref{ae2}, differencing again gives $\Delta_i^2B=4/(D(d_i+1)(d_i+2))>0$.  For Conjecture~\ref{ae3}, the linear part has vanishing mixed difference and $\Delta_i\Delta_j(2/D)=2/(D(d_i+1)(d_j+1))>0$.  For Conjecture~\ref{ae4}, writing $x=d_i$, $y=d_j$, $S=\sum_kd_k$, a direct expansion using $D\,D_{ij}=D_iD_j$ gives the exact identity
\[
B(\mathbf d+e_i+e_j)B(\mathbf d)-B(\mathbf d+e_i)B(\mathbf d+e_j)=-1+\frac{2(S+x+y-c)}{D(x+1)(y+1)},
\]
and the right side is negative: with $s_k=d_k-1$ and $R=\prod_{k\ne i,j}d_k$, one has $S+x+y-c=2x+2y-2+\sum's_k$, while $xy(x+1)(y+1)\ge6(x+y)$ and $R\ge1+\sum's_k$ give $D(x+1)(y+1)\ge6(x+y)+6(x+y)\sum's_k$, so the fraction is less than $1$ with room to spare.  For Conjecture~\ref{ae5}, at fixed $\sum_id_i$ and $c$ the linear part is constant and a balancing transfer $(x,y)\mapsto(x-1,y+1)$ with $x\ge y+2$ multiplies $D$ by $(x-1)(y+1)/(xy)>1$, so $u$ strictly decreases and $B$ is strictly Schur-convex.  For Conjecture~\ref{ae6}, a split $d\mapsto(a,b)$ with $a+b=d+1$ fixes the linear part and multiplies $D$ by $ab/d>1$, since $ab\ge2(d-1)\ge d+1$, so $B$ strictly decreases.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Hypersurface calibration for the convexity programme]\label{ae:hyper}
For a smooth hypersurface ($c=1$) of degree $d\ge2$ in $\mathbf P^{n+1}$, write $x=d-1$; then $B_{n,1}(d)=f_n(x)$ with $f_n(x)=(x^{n+2}+(-1)^nx)/(x+1)^2$, and $f_n$ is strictly increasing and strictly convex on $x\ge1$ for every $n\ge1$.  In particular Conjectures~\ref{ae1} and~\ref{ae2} hold at codimension one in every dimension.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The Chern-class formula gives $b_n^{\mathrm{prim}}=(-1)^n(\chi-(n+1))$ with $\chi=d\,[H^n](1+H)^{n+2}/(1+dH)$, and a direct evaluation of the residue yields $b_n^{\mathrm{prim}}=((d-1)^{n+2}+(-1)^n(d-1))/d$, so $B_{n,1}(d)=b_n^{\mathrm{prim}}/d=f_n(x)$ with $x=d-1$; for $n=1$ this is $(d-1)(d-2)/d$, matching Proposition~\ref{ae:curve}.  Differentiating, $(x+1)^3f_n'(x)=nx^{n+2}+(n+2)x^{n+1}+(-1)^n(1-x)$: for odd $n$ the last term is $x-1\ge0$, and for even $n$ the numerator is $x^{n+1}(nx+n+2)-(x-1)\ge x^{n+1}(nx+n+1)>0$ since $x-1\le x^{n+1}$, so $f_n'>0$ on $x\ge1$.  A second differentiation gives $(x+1)^4f_n''(x)=x^n\{n(n-1)x^2+2(n-1)(n+2)x+(n+1)(n+2)\}+2(-1)^n(x-2)$, whose bracket is positive and, times $x^n$, dominates the sign-varying correction $2(-1)^n(x-2)$ for every $n\ge1$ and $x\ge1$, so $f_n''>0$.  Strict positivity of $f_n'$ and $f_n''$ gives the strict first and second integer differences of Conjectures~\ref{ae1} and~\ref{ae2} at codimension one.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Antidiagonal calibration for the syzygy programme]\label{ae:strand}
Let $N+1=(a+1)(b+1)$ and $c_j=[t^j](1-t)^{N+1}\sum_{k\ge0}(ka+1)(kb+1)t^k$.  Then $\beta_{j-1,j}(a,b)-\beta_{j-2,j}(a,b)=(-1)^{j-1}c_j$ for every $j\ge2$, the resolution has length $N-2$, and $\beta_{N-2,N}=(a-1)(b-1)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The embedding is projectively normal, so the Hilbert series of the coordinate ring is $\sum_k\dim H^0(\mathcal O(ka,kb))\,t^k=\sum_k(ka+1)(kb+1)t^k$, and taking Euler characteristics of the minimal free resolution over the polynomial ring in $N+1$ variables gives $\sum_p(-1)^p\beta_{p,j}=c_j$ in every internal degree $j$.  Since $\beta_{p,j}$ vanishes unless $j-p\in\{0,1,2\}$, the degree-$j$ alternating sum collapses to the two displayed terms for $j\ge2$.  The coordinate ring is a normal semigroup ring, hence Cohen--Macaulay of dimension three and codimension $N-2$, so the resolution has length $N-2$ and the numerator $h(t)=(1-t)^3\sum_k(ka+1)(kb+1)t^k$ is a polynomial whose coefficients are third differences of a quadratic sequence: $h(t)=1+(N-2)t+(a-1)(b-1)t^2$ exactly.  Then $(1-t)^{N+1}\sum_k(ka+1)(kb+1)t^k=(1-t)^{N-2}h(t)$ has top coefficient $c_N=(-1)^{N-2}(a-1)(b-1)$, and since $\beta_{N-1,N}=0$ the degree-$N$ identity reads $(-1)^{N-2}\beta_{N-2,N}=c_N$, giving $\beta_{N-2,N}=(a-1)(b-1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Surface calibration for the dispersion programme]\label{ae:surface}
For $n=2$ set $x(d)=\pi_{2,d}(0)=\frac{(d-2)(d-3)}{6(d^2-3d+3)}$.  Then $x(d)$ is strictly increasing in $d\ge3$ with $x(d)<\tfrac16$ and $x(d)\to\tfrac16$, and consequently all four laws of Conjectures~\ref{ae12} to~\ref{ae15} hold for surfaces, strictly for $d\ge4$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For a smooth surface of degree $d$ one has $h_0=\binom{d-1}3$ and $\sum_jh_j=d^3-4d^2+6d-3=(d-1)(d^2-3d+3)$, giving the displayed $x(d)=\frac{(d-2)(d-3)}{6(d^2-3d+3)}$.  Its increment has the sign of $(2d-5)(d^2-3d+3)-(d^2-5d+6)(2d-3)=2d^2-6d+3>0$ for $d\ge3$, so $x$ is strictly increasing, and $x<\tfrac16$ is the inequality $(d-2)(d-3)<d^2-3d+3$, which reduces to $2d>3$.  The profile is $(x,1-2x,x)$ and $\varepsilon_2=(\tfrac16,\tfrac46,\tfrac16)$, so on three symmetric points every one of the four laws is equivalent to the monotone increase of $x$ below its limit $\tfrac16$: the likelihood ratio, the central mass $1-2x$, every convex functional, and $\|\pi_{2,d}-\varepsilon_2\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=2(\tfrac16-x)$ are all monotone in $x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Dispersion consequences of likelihood-ratio flattening]\label{ae:disp}
Conjecture~\ref{ae12} implies Conjectures~\ref{ae13} and~\ref{ae14}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The profile $\pi_{n,d}$ is symmetric about $n/2$.  Conjecture~\ref{ae12} is the monotone-likelihood-ratio order $\pi_{n,d}\le_{\mathrm{lr}}\pi_{n,d+1}$ on the common positive support, which for a symmetric profile is equivalent to the likelihood-ratio order of the centered displacement $R=|P-n/2|$; since likelihood-ratio order implies first-order stochastic dominance, $R$ under degree $d+1$ dominates $R$ under degree $d$, an outer position newly nonzero only strengthening the dominance.  Each central window $\{|P-n/2|\le\tfrac n2-k\}$ is a lower set for $R$, so its mass decreases, which is Conjecture~\ref{ae13}.  For any convex $\varphi$ the symmetrization $\psi(p)=\tfrac12(\varphi(p)+\varphi(n-p))$ is convex and nondecreasing in $R$, and symmetry gives $\mathbf E\varphi(P)=\mathbf E\psi(P)$; stochastic dominance of $R$ then yields $\mathbf E\varphi(\pi_{n,d})\le\mathbf E\varphi(\pi_{n,d+1})$, which is Conjecture~\ref{ae14}.
\end{proof}

\section{Normalized primitive cohomology of complete intersections}

\begin{conjecture}[Coordinate monotonicity of normalized complexity]\label{ae1}
For every $n\ge1$, $c\ge1$, every $\mathbf d\in\mathbf Z_{\ge2}^c$, and every coordinate $i$, $B_{n,c}(\mathbf d+e_i)>B_{n,c}(\mathbf d)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Raising one defining degree multiplies the raw topological size by the growing degree factor, and the conjecture asserts that the primitive middle cohomology outruns that trivial multiplicative scale in every dimension and codimension: normalized complexity has strictly positive marginal growth on the whole degree lattice.  The mechanism is transparent for curves, where Proposition~\ref{ae:curve} proves it from the exact formula, but the alternating Chern-class sum offers no visible positivity in higher dimension.  The nearest related results are the explicit primitive-Betti formulas of~\cite{GL02} and the Euler-characteristic implications of~\cite{CO74}, neither of which orders the degree lattice.  The hypersurface case, monotonicity at every $n$, is now proved in Proposition~\ref{ae:hyper}; a first decisive theorem in higher codimension would be codimension two.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $59{,}100$ coordinate steps on the exhaustive grid and $13{,}608$ steps on the extended adversarial grid passed, with no failure.  A counterexample would be a multidegree at which added degree is sublinear after normalization.

\begin{conjecture}[Strict discrete convexity in each degree]\label{ae2}
Under the same hypotheses, $B_{n,c}(\mathbf d+2e_i)-2B_{n,c}(\mathbf d+e_i)+B_{n,c}(\mathbf d)>0$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Beyond positive marginal growth, the marginal growth itself accelerates: each one-variable restriction of $B$ is strictly convex on the integer lattice, so normalized complexity bends upward in every defining degree.  The mechanism cannot be coefficientwise, since the Chern-class expression is alternating; Proposition~\ref{ae:curve} proves the curve case with second difference $4/(D(d_i+1)(d_i+2))$, a shape that suggests a positive rational generating function in general, and Proposition~\ref{ae:hyper} proves the hypersurface case in every dimension.  The nearest related result is~\cite{GL02}.  A first decisive theorem would be convexity for quadric-heavy multidegrees, where the formula degenerates.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $59{,}100$ second differences on the exhaustive grid and $13{,}608$ on the adversarial extension were strictly positive.  A counterexample would be one multidegree with a concave step, marking an unexpected cancellation in the Chern-class sum.

\begin{conjecture}[Additive supermodularity across degrees]\label{ae3}
For $i\ne j$, $B(\mathbf d+e_i+e_j)-B(\mathbf d+e_i)-B(\mathbf d+e_j)+B(\mathbf d)>0$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Distinct defining equations reinforce one another: raising $d_i$ makes a subsequent raise of $d_j$ strictly more valuable in absolute normalized complexity, so the discrete Hessian of $B$ is positive off the diagonal as well as on it.  Together with Conjecture~\ref{ae2} this asserts a full multivariate discrete convexity, and the curve case, mixed difference $2/(D(d_i+1)(d_j+1))$, is proved in Proposition~\ref{ae:curve}.  The nearest related results are~\cite{GL02,CO75}.  A first decisive theorem would be supermodularity at codimension two, where only one mixed pair exists.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $84{,}600$ mixed second differences on the exhaustive grid and $17{,}281$ on the adversarial extension were strictly positive.  A counterexample would be a pair of degrees whose interaction turns negative.

\begin{conjecture}[Strict log-submodularity]\label{ae4}
Whenever the four values are positive, $B(\mathbf d+e_i+e_j)\,B(\mathbf d)<B(\mathbf d+e_i)\,B(\mathbf d+e_j)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Set against Conjecture~\ref{ae3}, this is the striking pairing of the programme: absolute interaction of two degrees is positive while proportional interaction is negative, so $\log B$ is strictly submodular where $B$ is supermodular, the signature of diminishing relative returns familiar from discrete statistical mechanics and rare for a cohomological invariant.  The curve case follows from the exact identity of Proposition~\ref{ae:curve}, whose right side exposes the competition between the two orders.  The nearest related result is~\cite{GL02}.  A first decisive theorem would be log-submodularity for pairs of quadrics and cubics in all dimensions.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $84{,}600$ cross-products on the exhaustive grid and $17{,}281$ on the adversarial extension obeyed the strict inequality.  A counterexample would separate the two interaction orders at some multidegree, itself a sharp structural datum.

\begin{conjecture}[Schur-convexity at fixed degree sum]\label{ae5}
If $\mathbf d$ majorizes $\mathbf d'$ in $\mathbf Z_{\ge2}^c$ with equal coordinate sums, then $B_{n,c}(\mathbf d)\ge B_{n,c}(\mathbf d')$, strictly unless the vectors agree up to permutation.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Among complete intersections with the same dimension, codimension, and adjunction coefficient $\sum_id_i-(n+c+1)$, the balanced multidegrees minimize normalized primitive complexity and the lopsided ones maximize it: redistributing positivity unevenly enriches primitive topology even when the canonical class data are unchanged.  The unnormalized statement is false already for curves, where $b_1^{\mathrm{prim}}(2,4)=18<20=b_1^{\mathrm{prim}}(3,3)$, a retained control showing the normalization reverses the order; the normalized curve case is proved in Proposition~\ref{ae:curve} through the Schur-concavity of the degree product.  The nearest related results are the extremal Euler-characteristic theorems of~\cite{CO75}.  A first decisive theorem would be the single balancing transfer at codimension two.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $47{,}000$ balancing transfers on the exhaustive grid and $15{,}754$ on the adversarial extension strictly decreased $B$.  A counterexample would be a transfer at which balance raises normalized complexity.

\begin{conjecture}[Adjunction-preserving splits decrease complexity]\label{ae6}
For $d_i=d\ge3$ and $a,b\ge2$ with $a+b=d+1$, replacing the degree $d$ by the pair $(a,b)$ gives $B_{n,c+1}(\ldots,a,b,\ldots)<B_{n,c}(\ldots,d,\ldots)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The split raises the codimension by one while preserving the adjunction coefficient, so it moves between presentations that the canonical class cannot distinguish, and the conjecture orients this move: two lower-degree equations are strictly simpler per unit degree than one high-degree equation.  The unnormalized statement has no fixed direction, with $b_2^{\mathrm{prim}}(3)=6>5=b_2^{\mathrm{prim}}(2,2)$ against $b_1^{\mathrm{prim}}(4)=6<8=b_1^{\mathrm{prim}}(2,3)$, both retained as controls.  The split is the inverse of the merge order of Part~VII, and for odd $n$ its Calabi--Yau slice is already a theorem: there $B=E_n/D+(n+1)/D$, and both terms strictly increase under a merge, the first by Proposition~\ref{x:merge} and the second because merging strictly decreases the degree product, so the odd-dimensional Calabi--Yau case follows outright; the even-dimensional and general-adjunction cases are the open content.  The curve case is proved in Proposition~\ref{ae:curve}.  A first decisive theorem would be the even Calabi--Yau case, where the same two mechanisms compete.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $147{,}750$ admissible splits on the exhaustive grid and $346{,}825$ on the adversarial extension passed strictly.  A counterexample would be a split that concentrates rather than dilutes normalized topology.

\section{Controlled defects in Segre--Veronese syzygies}

\begin{conjecture}[Strict log-concavity of the nonlinear row]\label{ae7}
For every $a,b\ge2$ and every interior index $p$ of the positive support of the $q=2$ row, $\Delta^{(2)}_p>0$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The nonlinear row is exactly the row that resists the Gaussian heuristics of asymptotic syzygy theory, and the conjecture asserts that it nevertheless obeys the strongest local curvature law short of real-rootedness, strict log-concavity across its whole support.  The statement is stronger than the published unimodality conjecture for these rows~\cite{BCEGLY22}, which is the part's closest literature boundary and its attribution; the normality heuristic itself is~\cite{EEL15}, and log-concavity of syzygy rows is known to fail for small indices in other families~\cite{Park25}, so the claim is genuinely calibrated to this surface.  A first decisive theorem would be log-concavity of the three trailing entries, accessible from the tail formulas of~\cite{Lem21}.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $48$ interior triples of the thirteen complete published tables were strictly log-concave, the tables reverified file by file against the primary dataset and pinned by the antidiagonal identity of Proposition~\ref{ae:strand}; the statement rests on that small corpus.  A counterexample would be the first curvature pathology of a nonlinear row.

\begin{conjecture}[The linear row is log-concave through its mode]\label{ae8}
For every $a,b\ge2$ and every interior index $p\le m_1$ of the $q=1$ row, $\Delta^{(1)}_p>0$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Global log-concavity of the linear row is false, with the retained control $\beta_{14,15}^2-\beta_{13,14}\beta_{15,16}=-3{,}391{,}704$ at $\mathcal O(2,6)$, so the right law is one-sided: the ascending side and the mode keep strict log-concavity, and every observed failure sits deep in the descending tail.  The rising side is the regime where the finite tables are most compatible with the asymptotic normality picture of~\cite{EEL15}, and the conjecture extracts its most robust local consequence.  The nearest related results are~\cite{BCEGLY22,Lem21}.  A first decisive theorem would be log-concavity of the first three entries at every $(a,b)$, where binomial formulas for the low syzygies are available.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $102$ interior triples at or before the mode passed strictly across the thirteen tables; the small-corpus limit applies.  A counterexample would be a curvature reversal on the rising side, refuting the one-sided picture.

\begin{conjecture}[At most one defect in the linear row]\label{ae9}
For every $a,b\ge2$, the set $\{p:\Delta^{(1)}_p<0\}$ has at most one element.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Unimodality permits arbitrarily many local curvature reversals; this conjecture forbids all but one, asserting that the linear row is a nearly totally positive sequence with a single controlled exception.  Across the thirteen published tables, five rows have no defect and eight have exactly one, at indices $14,16,18,20,22$ for $\mathcal O(2,b)$, $b=6,\ldots,10$, and $14,16,19$ for $\mathcal O(3,b)$, $b=4,5,6$, an arithmetic progression pattern in the first family that any proof should explain.  The nearest related results are~\cite{BCEGLY22,Park25}.  A first decisive theorem would be uniqueness of the defect for $\mathcal O(2,b)$, the family with the cleanest tail formulas~\cite{Lem21}.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, no table carried two defects; the small-corpus limit applies.  A counterexample would be a linear row with two curvature reversals, breaking the controlled-defect picture.

\begin{conjecture}[Defects occur only inside the nonlinear overlap]\label{ae10}
For every $a,b\ge2$, if $\Delta^{(1)}_p<0$ then $\beta_{p,p+2}(a,b)>0$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The conjecture couples a shape property of one row to nonvanishing in the next: the linear row can lose log-concavity only at homological positions where nonlinear syzygies are already present, so a vanishing theorem for $K_{p,2}$ would automatically restore strict log-concavity of $K_{p,1}$ there.  All eight observed defects obey the coupling, and the rational-normal-scroll boundary $a=1$, where the nonlinear row is empty, has defect-free linear rows across the eight published scroll tables, consistent with the picture from outside the stated range.  The nearest related results are~\cite{BCEGLY22,EEL15}.  A first decisive theorem would be defect-freeness wherever the nonlinear row vanishes, a statement about the 2-linear part alone.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, the coupling held in all eight defect tables; the small-corpus limit applies.  A counterexample would be a defect before the nonlinear row enters, decoupling the two rows.

\begin{conjecture}[Defect-mode locking]\label{ae11}
For every $a,b\ge2$, if the linear row has a defect at $p_{*}$ then $p_{*}\in\{m_2,m_2+1\}$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
This is the boldest statement of the syzygy programme: the unique loss of curvature in the linear row is phase-locked to the concentration point of the nonlinear row, landing at its mode or one step beyond in every observed table, exactly at $m_2$ for $\mathcal O(2,b)$ and at $m_2$ or $m_2+1$ for $\mathcal O(3,b)$.  A proof would exhibit a cross-row mechanism in minimal resolutions that no current theory predicts; even a failure would be valuable, since the displacement $p_{*}-m_2$ is a sharp statistic to track across embeddings.  The nearest related results are~\cite{BCEGLY22,EEL15,Lem21}.  A first decisive theorem would be the locking for $\mathcal O(2,b)$, where both rows have explicit tails.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, the locking held in all eight defect tables; this statement rests on the small corpus, whose limits apply with full force.  A counterexample would be a defect drifting away from the nonlinear mode.

\section{Monotone dispersion of hypersurface Hodge profiles}

\begin{conjecture}[Likelihood-ratio flattening in the degree]\label{ae12}
For every $n\ge2$, $d\ge3$, and $0\le p<q\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, $h_p(n,d+1)\,h_q(n,d)\ge h_p(n,d)\,h_q(n,d+1)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
As the degree grows, outer Hodge pieces gain relative weight against pieces nearer the middle, uniformly in every pair of positions: a monotone likelihood-ratio comparison between the Hodge structures of different varieties.  The coefficient vector is a convolution of discrete uniforms, but the sampling lattice moves with the degree, so no fixed-lattice total-positivity argument applies directly; the surface case is proved in Proposition~\ref{ae:surface}.  Equalities occur while an outer piece is still zero, so the non-strict form is the uniform statement.  The nearest related results are~\cite{Gri69,DK86}.  A first decisive theorem would be the outermost pair $(0,1)$ at every $n$, the geometric-genus-to-next-piece ratio.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $71{,}920$ cross-products on the grid and $164{,}502$ on the extension passed.  A counterexample would be a degree step at which the profile sharpens toward the center.

\begin{conjecture}[Central-window escape]\label{ae13}
For every $n\ge2$, $d\ge3$, and $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, $\sum_{p=k}^{n-k}\pi_{n,d+1}(p)\le\sum_{p=k}^{n-k}\pi_{n,d}(p)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Every central window of the Hodge diamond loses normalized mass monotonically as the degree grows: cohomology drains from the middle toward the outer pieces at every scale simultaneously, a position-sensitive statement strictly stronger than growth of any single spread functional.  The mechanism is the same moving-lattice convolution as Conjecture~\ref{ae12}, of which this is a consequence for symmetric profiles, proved in Proposition~\ref{ae:disp}; the surface case is Proposition~\ref{ae:surface}.  The nearest related results are~\cite{Gri69,LS25}.  A first decisive theorem would be the innermost window $k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, the central Hodge piece alone.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $13{,}050$ window comparisons on the grid and $25{,}272$ on the extension passed.  A counterexample would be a window recapturing mass at some degree step.

\begin{conjecture}[Convex-order dispersion]\label{ae14}
For every $n\ge2$ and $d\ge3$, the profile $\pi_{n,d}$ precedes $\pi_{n,d+1}$ in convex order.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The degree flow is a mean-preserving spread: every convex functional of the normalized Hodge position, the variance, all even central moments, every exponential moment, increases weakly at each degree step, so infinitely many numerical Hodge inequalities are packaged into one canonical stochastic order.  Like Conjecture~\ref{ae13}, this order is a consequence of Conjecture~\ref{ae12} for symmetric profiles (Proposition~\ref{ae:disp}): the window comparisons give stochastic dominance of the centered displacement, and symmetrizing a convex statistic reduces the convex order to that dominance.  On finite symmetric support the order is equivalent to the call-function comparisons $\mathbf E(P-t)_+$, which is how it is tested exactly; the surface case is Proposition~\ref{ae:surface}, and the only coincident consecutive profiles in the tested range are the cubic and quartic threefolds.  The nearest related results are~\cite{Gri69,DK86}.  A first decisive theorem would be the variance alone, the second-moment shadow of the order.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, all $1{,}682$ degree transitions on the grid and $2{,}730$ on the extension passed.  A counterexample would be a convex statistic moving against the spread.

\begin{conjecture}[Monotone total-variation convergence to the Eulerian profile]\label{ae15}
For every $n\ge2$ and $d\ge3$, $\|\pi_{n,d+1}-\varepsilon_n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\|\pi_{n,d}-\varepsilon_n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$, with equality only at $(n,d)=(3,3)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The normalized profiles drift toward the Eulerian distribution, exactly the law of descents of a random permutation of $n+1$ letters; the conjecture upgrades that drift to monotone convergence in total variation from the first degree onward, a finite-degree error principle that one verified threshold would convert into bounds at every larger degree.  Convergence alone forces no monotonicity, and the coordinatewise strengthening is false, a retained control: at $n=12$ the $p=5$ mass crosses its Eulerian limit between degrees six and seven and overshoots, so the cancellation across positions asserted here is the genuine content.  The Eulerian limit is exact for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties~\cite{LS25}, asymptotic in the toric setting~\cite{DK86}, and feeds effective arithmetic applications~\cite{Ji24}; only the monotone interpolation is claimed.  A first decisive theorem would be a one-crossing law between $\pi_{n,d}$ and $\varepsilon_n$.  In tests on the corpus described in the stress-test section, the distance never increased across $1{,}682$ grid and $2{,}730$ extension transitions, the sole equality being the cubic--quartic threefold coincidence.  A counterexample would be a degree step moving the profile away from the Eulerian law.


\part{Stochastic order, curvature, and dependence laws for self-avoiding walks}

\medskip\noindent\emph{Added to the deposit: 19 August 2026.}\par\medskip

The fifteen conjectures below concern the uniform measure on $n$-step self-avoiding walks on the hypercubic lattice, the classical model whose most basic monotonicity questions, including whether the mean-square displacement grows with the length, remain open~\cite{MS93,BDGS12}.  They form four programmes.  A curvature programme (Conjectures~\ref{af1} to~\ref{af3}) asserts exact all-length curvature laws for three count sequences: the square-lattice counts $c_n$ are strictly log-concave in steps of two with curvature relaxing monotonically to zero, sharpening the ratio analysis of Hammersley's programme carried out by Guttmann and Jensen~\cite{GJ22}; every radial-moment sum $M_q(n)$ obeys the same parity log-concavity at every real order $q\ge0$; and the bridge counts $b_n$ obey the opposite law, strict log-convexity from $n=5$ onward, so that walk ratios would descend to $\mu^2$ while bridge ratios ascend to $\mu$.  A transport programme (Conjectures~\ref{af4} to~\ref{af8}) asserts stochastic-order growth in the length: likelihood-ratio growth of the bridge height and of the coordinate span, coordinatewise monotone couplings of the absolute endpoint vector and of the span vector under $n\to n+2$, and stochastic growth of the contact count; the endpoint coupling strictly implies the open mean-square-displacement monotonicity along each parity class.  A dependence programme (Conjectures~\ref{af9} to~\ref{af12}) assigns signs to four joint laws at every fixed length: the two spans are negatively quadrant dependent, radius and terminal atmosphere positively, radius and contacts negatively, and contacts and atmosphere negatively, an extension--compaction dependence structure for a measure with no known FKG-type property.  A phase-and-dimension programme (Conjectures~\ref{af13} to~\ref{af15}) states a partition-curvature trichotomy across the collapse transition whose three constants are the established predictions of~\cite{Nie82,DS87,OPB93}, and two strict cross-dimensional laws: the probability that a nonbacktracking walk is self-avoiding rises with the dimension at every fixed length, and every positive radial moment falls.  The proved layer is three calibrations: Proposition~\ref{af:extreme} proves the extreme-order regime of both moment laws from a two-walk extremal count and a spanning-axes inequality $c_n(d+1)>(1+1/d)\,c_n(d)$; Proposition~\ref{af:height} computes the top four diagonals of the bridge-height array in closed form and proves the top corner of the likelihood-ratio law at every length; and Proposition~\ref{af:nbw} computes the survival probabilities $q_{d,n}$ for $n\le7$ as explicit rational functions of $d$ and proves Conjecture~\ref{af14} there in every dimension at once; and Proposition~\ref{af:rad2} proves Conjecture~\ref{af15} at length two for every dimension and every positive moment order.  Four negative controls are retained in place: the absolute endpoint coordinates are not negatively quadrant dependent already at $n=3$, so the span law of Conjecture~\ref{af9} is not a symmetry artifact; the full radial distributions cross between adjacent dimensions, so the moment formulation of Conjecture~\ref{af15} is forced; bridge log-convexity fails exactly at $n=2$ and $n=4$, so the threshold of Conjecture~\ref{af3} is sharp; and the finite-size roots of the curvature diagnostic of Conjecture~\ref{af13} oscillate below $n\approx12$, so that statement is asymptotic only.  Conjecture~\ref{af1} is the part's closest to prior work: its statistic and its asymptotics are explicitly Guttmann--Jensen's~\cite{GJ22}, and only the exact strict inequalities and the second-level monotonicity are proposed as new; Conjecture~\ref{af13} is a consolidation, since each of its three regimes is separately the standard prediction and the new content is the uniform sequence-level formulation.

An $n$-step self-avoiding walk on $\mathbf Z^d$ is a nearest-neighbour path $\omega=(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_n)$, $\omega_0=0$, with distinct vertices; $c_n(d)$ is their number, $c_n=c_n(2)$, and $U_n$ is the uniform measure on the square-lattice walks, whose connective constant is $\mu=\lim c_n^{1/n}\approx2.63815853$.  Write $\omega_n=(X_n,Y_n)$, $R_n^2=|\omega_n|^2$, $M_q(n)=\sum_\omega|\omega_n|^q$, and let $S_x,S_y$ be the coordinate spans $\max_i x_i-\min_i x_i$ and its $y$-analogue.  The terminal atmosphere $A_n\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ is the number of unvisited neighbours of $\omega_n$; since every $(n+1)$-step walk extends a unique $n$-step walk, $\sum_\omega A_n(\omega)=c_{n+1}$, so $\mathbf E[A_n]=c_{n+1}/c_n$ exactly, the identity underlying atmospheric sampling methods~\cite{RJvR08,OP08}.  The contact count $C_n$ is the number of nonbonded nearest-neighbour pairs of visited vertices, with partition function $Z_n(u)=\sum_\omega u^{C_n(\omega)}$ for the interacting walk~\cite{BOS01,BGJ20}.  A bridge is a walk with $x_0=0$, $x_i\ge1$ for $i\ge1$, and $x_i\le x_n$ for all $i$; $b_n$ counts them, $B(n,h)$ counts those of height $x_n=h$, and $b_1,\ldots,b_{10}=1,3,7,17,41,101,251,631,1591,4029$, with $b_mb_n\le b_{m+n}$ and $b_n^{1/n}\to\mu$ by Hammersley--Welsh unfolding~\cite{HW62}.  A uniformly random $n$-step nonbacktracking walk on $\mathbf Z^d$ is self-avoiding with probability $q_{d,n}=c_n(d)/(2d(2d-1)^{n-1})$~\cite{FvdH13}.  For laws $P,Q$ on $\mathbf Z$ or $\mathbf Z^2$, $P\le_{\mathrm{st}}Q$ means $Q$ dominates $P$ on upper sets, equivalently a coupling exists with the $Q$-variable coordinatewise at least the $P$-variable; $\le_{\mathrm{lr}}$ is likelihood-ratio order, the total positivity of the two-row array; and $(X,Y)$ is positively (negatively) quadrant dependent when $\mathbf P(X\ge a,Y\ge b)$ is at least (at most) $\mathbf P(X\ge a)\mathbf P(Y\ge b)$ for all thresholds.  All finite verifications below are exact: integer enumeration, integer cross-products, and integer maximum flows for the coupling laws, with the full joint laws enumerated through $n=21$ ($c_{21}=2{,}408{,}806{,}028$ walks at the top length), bridges through $n=23$, dimensions through $d=10$, and published counts through $n=79$~\cite{Jen13}.

\begin{proposition}[Extreme-order calibration for the moment laws]\label{af:extreme}
(i) For all $n\ge2$ and $d\ge1$, $c_n(d+1)>(1+1/d)\,c_n(d)$.  (ii) For every $n\ge3$ there is $q_0(n)$ such that $M_q(n)^2>M_q(n-2)M_q(n+2)$ for all real $q\ge q_0(n)$.  (iii) For every $n\ge2$ and $d\ge2$ there is $q_1(n,d)$ such that $\mathbf E_{d+1}[R_n^q]<\mathbf E_d[R_n^q]$ for all real $q\ge q_1(n,d)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) Group walks by the set of coordinate axes their steps use: $c_n(d)=\sum_{k\ge1}\binom dk s_{n,k}$, where $s_{n,k}$ counts $n$-step walks in $\mathbf Z^k$ using all $k$ axes.  Since $\binom{d+1}k/\binom dk=(d+1)/(d+1-k)\ge(d+1)/d$ for $k\ge1$, strictly for $k\ge2$, and $s_{n,2}>0$ for $n\ge2$, the sum grows strictly faster than the factor $(d+1)/d$.  (ii) Exactly $2d$ walks, the straight ones, attain $|\omega_n|=n$; every other walk has $|\omega_n|^2\le n^2-2n+2$, since $|x|+|y|\le n$ with $|x|\le n-1$ forces $x^2+y^2\le(n-1)^2+1$.  Hence $M_q(n)=4n^q(1+\delta_n(q))$ on the square lattice with $0\le\delta_n(q)\le\tfrac{c_n}4\theta_n^q$ and $\theta_n=\sqrt{n^2-2n+2}/n<1$, so
\[
\frac{M_q(n)^2}{M_q(n-2)M_q(n+2)}\ \ge\ \Bigl(\frac{n^2}{n^2-4}\Bigr)^{\!q}\,\frac1{(1+\delta_{n-2}(q))(1+\delta_{n+2}(q))}\ \longrightarrow\ \infty
\]
as $q\to\infty$.  (iii) Likewise $\mathbf E_d[R_n^q]=(2d\,n^q/c_n(d))(1+\delta)$ with $\delta\to0$, so the ratio of consecutive-dimension moments tends to $\frac{(d+1)\,c_n(d)}{d\,c_n(d+1)}$, which is strictly below $1$ by (i).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Top-corner calibration for the bridge programme]\label{af:height}
For all admissible $n$, $B(n,n)=1$, $B(n,n-1)=2(n-1)$, $B(n,n-2)=2(n-2)^2$, and $B(n,n-3)=\tfrac23(n-3)(2n^2-12n+19)$; consequently the top two adjacent cross-products of Conjecture~\ref{af4} hold at every length:
\begin{align*}
B(n,n{-}1)B(n{+}1,n)-B(n,n)B(n{+}1,n{-}1)&=2(n-1)(n+1),\\
B(n,n{-}2)B(n{+}1,n{-}1)-B(n,n{-}1)B(n{+}1,n{-}2)&=\tfrac43(n-2)(n-1)(n^2-n-3),
\end{align*}
both positive for $n\ge2$ and $n\ge3$ respectively.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A bridge of height $n-k$ with $v$ vertical steps and $m$ backward horizontal steps has $n=h+2m+v$, so $k=2m+v$.  If $m\ge1$ and $v=0$ the walk lives on the axis and a backward step revisits it; if $m=1$ and $v=1$, the backward step must immediately follow the vertical step, since anything else backtracks or revisits the axis, after which any forward step re-enters the column just left, while placing the backward step last makes the running maximum $n-2$ exceed $x_n=n-3$; so all horizontal steps point forward and $v=k$ for $k\le3$.  The $x$-coordinate is then nondecreasing, distinct columns never collide, and within a column a vertical run is self-avoiding exactly when its signs are constant, so the count is $\sum_r N_r2^r$ over placements of the $k$ vertical steps into the $n-1$ slots after the forced first step, $N_r$ the number of placements with $r$ maximal runs.  For $k=1,2,3$ this gives $2(n-1)$, $4\binom{n-1}2-2(n-2)=2(n-2)^2$, and $2(n-3)+8\binom{n-3}2+8\binom{n-3}3=\tfrac23(n-3)(2n^2-12n+19)$.  The two displayed identities are then polynomial algebra, and their factorizations are positive on the stated ranges.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Survival calibration in every dimension]\label{af:nbw}
For all $d\ge2$,
\[
1-q_{d,4}=\frac{2(d-1)}{(2d-1)^3},\qquad
1-q_{d,5}=\frac{2(d-1)(4d-3)}{(2d-1)^4},\qquad
1-q_{d,6}=\frac{8(d-1)(3d^2-2d-2)}{(2d-1)^5},
\]
\[
1-q_{d,7}=\frac{2(d-1)(32d^3-28d^2-46d+41)}{(2d-1)^6},
\]
and each $q_{d,n}$, $4\le n\le7$, is strictly increasing in $d$ on all of $d\ge2$; Conjecture~\ref{af14} therefore holds for $n\le7$ in every dimension.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A nonbacktracking walk of length at most $5$ fails to be self-avoiding only through a four-cycle among steps $1$--$4$ or steps $2$--$5$; counting the two events and their intersection (which forces the fifth step to repeat the first) gives $c_4(d)=2d(2d-1)^3-2d(2d-2)$ and $c_5(d)=2d(2d-1)^4-2d(2d-2)(4d-3)$, whence the first two displays.  For $n=6,7$, the axis-grouping identity $c_n(d)=\sum_k\binom dk s_{n,k}$ of Proposition~\ref{af:extreme} expresses $c_n$ as a polynomial in $d$ of degree $n$ determined by exact enumeration in $\mathbf Z^k$ for $k\le n$; this gives $c_6(d)=64d^6-160d^5+112d^4+20d^2-34d$ and $c_7(d)=128d^7-384d^6+352d^5-80d^4+192d^3-372d^2+166d$, agreeing with the classical $1/d$-expansion polynomials of Fisher and Gaunt~\cite{FG64} and reverified here against direct enumeration for $2\le d\le10$.  For each $n\le7$ the difference $q_{d+1,n}-q_{d,n}$ is a rational function whose denominator is positive and whose numerator, expanded in $t=d-2$, has every coefficient nonnegative and constant term positive (for $n=4$ the numerator is $32t^3+168t^2+280t+142$), so the difference is strictly positive for all real $d\ge2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Radial moments at length two]\label{af:rad2}
For $n=2$, every $d\ge2$, and every real $q>0$, $\mathbf E_{U_2^{(d)}}[|\omega_2|^q]=2^{q/2}+(2^q-2^{q/2})/(2d-1)$, strictly decreasing in $d$; in particular Conjecture~\ref{af15} holds at $n=2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A two-step self-avoiding walk on $\Z^d$ is a nonbacktracking walk: conditional on the first step, one of the $2d-1$ continuations is straight, with $|\omega_2|=2$, and the other $2d-2$ turn, with $|\omega_2|=\sqrt2$.  Averaging $|\omega_2|^q$ over the uniform choice gives $(2^q+(2d-2)2^{q/2})/(2d-1)=2^{q/2}+(2^q-2^{q/2})/(2d-1)$, and since $2^q>2^{q/2}$ for $q>0$ the second term strictly decreases in $d$.
\end{proof}

\section{Curvature laws for counts, radial moments, and bridges}

\begin{conjecture}[Parity log-concavity and curvature relaxation of walk counts]\label{af1}
For $\rho_n=c_{n+2}c_{n-2}/c_n^2$ and every $n\ge2$: $0<\rho_n<1$ and $\rho_n<\rho_{n+2}<1$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
The statement says that $\log c_n$ is strictly concave in steps of two and that its discrete curvature relaxes monotonically to zero: the two-step ratios $c_{n+2}/c_n$ decrease strictly along each parity class onto their limit $\mu^2$, so each would be a certified upper bound on $\mu^2$ improving monotonically, complementing O'Brien's monotonicity $c_{n+1}\ge c_n$~\cite{OBr90}, with the ratio limit and its $n^{-1/3}$ rate Kesten's~\cite{Kes63}.  This conjecture is the part's closest to prior work: the statistic $\rho_n$ and its asymptotics $\rho_n\sim1-4(\gamma-1)/n^2=1-11/(8n^2)$ are exactly the objects of Guttmann and Jensen's analysis of Hammersley's programme~\cite{GJ22} with the exponent $\gamma=43/32$ of~\cite{Nie82}, and monotonicity hypotheses of this type are the assumptions under which they derive the existence of critical exponents; the exact strict all-$n$ inequalities and the second-level claim that the curvature itself is monotone are the content proposed here.  A first decisive theorem would be $\rho_n<1$ for all $n$, a strict two-step Fekete inequality beyond submultiplicativity.  In tests against the published counts through $n=79$~\cite{Jen13}, every $\rho_n$ and every increment obeys both inequalities, the largest $\rho_{77}=0.99977583$; a violation at large $n$ would show correction terms overturning the scaling curvature after its apparent onset.

\begin{conjecture}[Radial-moment parity log-concavity at every order]\label{af2}
For every real $q\ge0$ and every $n\ge3$, $M_q(n)^2>M_q(n-2)M_q(n+2)$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
At $q=0$ this is the concavity clause of Conjecture~\ref{af1}; the conjecture extends it to the entire Mellin family of endpoint-weighted counts, whose predicted growth $M_q(n)\sim A_q\mu^nn^{\gamma-1+q\nu}$ with $\nu=3/4$~\cite{Nie82} always carries a positive polynomial exponent, so the scaling curvature $-4(\gamma-1+q\nu)/n^2$ is negative at every order.  Since $c_n\le M_q(n)\le n^qc_n$ for $q>0$, each $M_q$ has growth constant $\mu$, and the conjecture would produce an infinite hierarchy of metric-weighted two-step ratios decreasing onto $\mu^2$, upper bounds that see endpoint geometry.  Proposition~\ref{af:extreme} proves the extreme-order regime: for each $n$ the inequality holds for all sufficiently large $q$, by the two-walk extremal count at radius $n$.  The metric series themselves are enumerated to great length in~\cite{Jen13}; no moment-sum log-concavity statement appears there or elsewhere located.  A first decisive theorem would be the law at $q=2$, the mean-square-displacement-weighted count.  In exact tests at $q\in\{0,2,4,6,8\}$ and on a grid of $501$ orders through $q=50$, all lengths $n\le20$ pass, minimum ratio $1.00413$; a counterexample would exhibit an order at which endpoint weighting overturns coefficient curvature.

\begin{conjecture}[Eventual strict log-convexity of bridge counts]\label{af3}
For every $n\ge5$, $b_n^2<b_{n-1}b_{n+1}$.
\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Significance.}
Bridges are predicted to grow as $b_n\sim B\mu^nn^{\gamma_b-1}$ with the negative polynomial exponent $\gamma_b-1=-7/16$~\cite{DG19}, so their logarithmic curvature $+7/(16n^2)$ has the opposite sign to Conjecture~\ref{af1}: walk ratios would fall to $\mu^2$ while bridge ratios rise to $\mu$, squeezing the connective constant from both sides.  The conjecture upgrades that prediction to an exact inequality from the sharp threshold onward; the negative control is exact, $b_2^2-b_1b_3=b_4^2-b_3b_5=2$, so log-convexity fails at $n=2$ and $n=4$ and at no other tested length.  Under the conjecture the ratios $b_{n+1}/b_n$ increase, and since $b_n^{1/n}\to\mu$~\cite{HW62} they increase onto $\mu$, so each ratio is a certified lower bound; supermultiplicativity~\cite{HW62} gives no pointwise convexity, and Kesten's irreducible-bridge renewal structure~\cite{Kes63} suggests the natural route, since Kaluza-type theorems derive log-convexity from renewal representations.
